plan:
EXPERIMENT DESIGN — Throughput vs. Microbatch Count for 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p (ZB-H1), and ZB-2p (ZB-H2)

DESIGN-ONLY DELIVERABLE. No experiment was executed; no results are claimed. The /workspace repository contains no code (verified: only task.json; track.md states "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required"), so all schedule logic below is grounded in the Zero Bubble Pipeline Parallelism paper (Qi et al., ICLR 2024) and its Megatron-LM fork conventions.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. RESEARCH QUESTION AND TESTABLE PREDICTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────
Question: Does throughput of 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p improve as the number of microbatches m increases, while ZB-2p maintains high throughput even at small m?

Hypotheses stated as testable predictions (reference points from analytical formulas, not foregone conclusions):
- P1 (1F1B): iteration time T = (m + p − 1)(t_f + t_b); bubble fraction (p−1)/(m+p−1) shrinks with m, so throughput improves monotonically with m and asymptotes at m ≫ p.
- P2 (1F1B-I, interleaved with V model chunks per rank): same monotone improvement with m; at equal m ≥ warmup needs, bubble is reduced by roughly a factor of the interleaving depth versus 1F1B, but warmup depth scales with the chunk structure, so 1F1B-I is expected to be MORE sensitive to small m than non-interleaved 1F1B (tested, not assumed).
- P3 (ZB-1p / ZB-H1): eliminates Type-II bubbles (the backward-dependent portion) but retains warmup-dependent bubbles, whose reference form is ≈ (p−1)·t_f per rank versus 1F1B's (p−1)(t_f+t_b). Prediction: throughput improves with m (bubble fraction ≈ (p−1)t_f / (m(t_f+t_b) + (p−1)t_f)) while remaining strictly above 1F1B at equal m; the advantage grows as t_b/t_f grows.
- P4 (ZB-2p / ZB-H2): near-zero bubble already at m ≈ p (the paper's central claim), i.e., throughput nearly flat in m across the sweep, at the cost of extra in-flight activation buffers. One sentence note: the paper also defines an interleaved extension ZB-H2-I (ZB-2p-I), which is out of scope as a primary method here.
- P5 (composite): the qualitative ranking at m = p is ZB-2p > ZB-1p > 1F1B ≈ 1F1B-I-or-worse; at large m the four methods converge.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. INSTRUMENT: DETERMINISTIC EVENT-DRIVEN SCHEDULE SIMULATOR
────────────────────────────────────────
A discrete-event simulator (pure Python stdlib, CPU-only) constructs each schedule's timeline from its paper definition:
- 1F1B: warmup depth p − rank − 1 forwards before steady-state 1F-1B alternation; cooldown drains remaining backwards.
- 1F1B-I: V model chunks per rank, Megatron-style warmup formula (per-chunk warmup of (p − 1) scaled by chunk position); forward/backward events alternate across chunks. Constraint honored in the sweep: m must be divisible by V.
- ZB-1p (ZB-H1): allows a backward to be scheduled before the matching send-forward completes per the paper's dependency relaxation (B passes depend on the corresponding F's output availability for loss, but the send to the next stage is decoupled), eliminating Type-II bubbles; warmup depth p − 1 like 1F1B but with T-type passes allowed in warmup.
- ZB-2p (ZB-H2): additionally permits double-forward (2F) scheduling enabled by an extra in-flight activation buffer per rank, achieving zero total bubble in the idealized setting. Per the paper's buffer analysis, ZB-H2 requires at most one additional in-flight activation per rank versus ZB-H1; the simulator will enforce the paper's warmup/buffer discipline and record, rather than assume, the minimum m at which the zero-bubble property holds (prediction: m ≥ p suffices; m < p degenerates as warmup dominates).
Each event carries (rank, pass type, chunk, start, duration); the scheduler greedily dispatches ready events respecting the dependency rules of that method. Time is discrete on a fine common grid so all methods share the same clock granularity.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. METRIC DEFINITIONS (same scale for all four methods)
────────────────────────────────────────
(a) Throughput, primary: TP = m / T_iter, i.e., microbatches completed per unit simulated wall-clock time per pipeline (T_iter = end-to-end time of one full iteration = makespan across all ranks). Secondary, scale-free: normalized efficiency η = (m·(t_f+t_b)) / (p·T_iter) — work done per rank divided by the ideal p-rank execution time; η = 1 means a perfectly filled pipeline.
(b) Bubble fraction, consistently defined: BF = total_idle / (p·T_iter) = 1 − η, where total_idle = Σ_rank (T_iter − busy_time_rank) and busy_time counts only forward/backward compute (communication excluded per the simplifying assumption below). BF and η are algebraically linked, giving one coherent scale across 1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p.
Also logged per cell: per-rank idle histograms (to locate warmup/cooldown vs. mid-iteration bubbles), max in-flight activations per rank (ZB-H2 buffer cost), and, for ZB-2p, the smallest m at which BF ≤ 1% is achieved.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. VARIABLES AND SWEEP (including small m)
────────────────────────────────────────
Manipulated: method ∈ {1F1B, 1F1B-I, ZB-1p, ZB-2p}; m ∈ {⌈p/2⌉ (degenerate probe), p, 2p, 4p, 8p} — the sweep deliberately includes m at and below the practical minimum so ZB-2p's small-m behavior is directly tested, not extrapolated.
Controlled: p ∈ {4, 8, 16}; t_f:t_b ratio ∈ {1:1, 1:2, 1:4} (t_f = 1.0 time unit normalized; t_b = 2·t_f as the headline configuration, matching the paper's typical backward ≈ 2× forward); interleaving depth V = 4 chunks per rank for 1F1B-I (m restricted to multiples of V; this constraint is reported when it bites, e.g., m = p with p = 8 gives only 2 microbatches per chunk); communication = zero for all methods (simplifying assumption, resolved by the researcher); identical per-microbatch FLOPs across methods.
Grid size: 4 methods × 3 p × 5 m × 3 ratios = 180 simulator runs (with divisibility exclusions for 1F1B-I), each run milliseconds — a few seconds total on system Python.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. FAIR-COMPARISON PROTOCOL
────────────────────────────────────────
- Identical per-microbatch compute cost (t_f, t_b) and identical stage count p across methods in every comparison.
- When throughput is compared across methods at different m, comparisons are made (i) at equal m (pure schedule-quality comparison) and (ii) at equal global batch via a secondary scaling analysis (throughput per token: TP × microbatch token size, fixed). Headline claims use (i); (ii) shows whether ZB-2p's flat curve translates into practical small-batch wins.
- Warmup policy fixed per method exactly as defined in the paper; no ad-hoc tuning per cell.
- ZB-2p's extra buffer memory is reported as an overhead column but excluded from timing (memory does not enter the simulated clock).
- Identical event-grid granularity and zero-communication treatment for all methods.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────
Across t_f:t_b ∈ {1:1, 1:2, 1:4} and p ∈ {4, 8, 16}, report a qualitative-conclusion matrix: which predictions (P1–P5) hold in every cell and which are ratio- or depth-dependent. Expected outcomes to be tested: (i) P4 (ZB-2p near-zero bubble at m ≈ p) should be robust to all settings since it is warmup-structure-driven; (ii) P3's ZB-1p-over-1F1B gap should widen with t_b/t_f because the eliminated Type-II bubble is proportional to t_b; (iii) at t_f:t_b = 1:1 the ZB-1p advantage shrinks toward parity with 1F1B, which is a genuine finding if observed, not a failure; (iv) 1F1B-I's small-m degradation (deeper warmup) should be visible at p = 16, V = 4. The design explicitly treats any non-robust conclusions as reportable results.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDATION PLAN
────────────────────────────────────────
- V1 (1F1B exactness): assert simulated T_iter = (m + p − 1)(t_f + t_b) and BF = (p−1)/(m+p−1) at large m (m ≥ 4p) for all p and ratios; any deviation indicates a scheduler bug.
- V2 (1F1B-I sanity): at large m, simulated BF should approach (p−1)(t_f+t_b)/(V·m·(t_f+t_b) + (p−1)(t_f+t_b)) — i.e., roughly a V-fold reduction versus 1F1B at equal m — and per-rank idle should be concentrated at the warmup head and cooldown tail with no mid-iteration gaps.
- V3 (ZB-1p): simulated BF at large m should match the reference (p−1)t_f/(m(t_f+t_b)+(p−1)t_f) within the time-grid tolerance.
- V4 (ZB-2p): BF ≤ 1% for m ≥ p across all ratio/p cells; log the observed minimum-m threshold against the paper's buffer analysis rather than assuming it.
- V5 (cross-check): qualitative trend comparison against the paper's reported bubble/throughput figures (1F1B, interleaved, ZB-H1, ZB-H2 curves).

────────────────────────────────────────
8. CONTROLS, THREATS TO VALIDITY
────────────────────────────────────────
Controls: fixed per-microbatch cost across methods; equal global batch in the secondary comparison; paper-defined warmup policies; identical clock grid; zero and identical communication; p and ratio swept jointly for both methods in every pairwise comparison.
Threats to validity (stated, not hidden): (1) idealized zero communication and no overlap modeling — real 1F1B-I pays more communication per microbatch than non-interleaved, so real-world 1F1B-I may look worse than simulated; (2) no memory-bandwidth or kernel-launch effects; uniform, straggler-free stage costs; (3) ZB-H2's exact warmup/buffer discipline at small m is reconstructed from the paper's description and the fork's conventions — the V4 check mitigates but cannot eliminate this; (4) analytic reference formulas are approximations for small m (warmup-dominated regime), so simulator-vs-formula discrepancies at m ≈ p are themselves informative; (5) results are for the idealized single-pipeline model, not any specific model architecture (though the appendix maps parameters onto a real model's measured t_f/t_b).

────────────────────────────────────────
9. ANALYSIS PLAN
────────────────────────────────────────
Primary output: a table and plot of TP (and BF) versus m for each method at the headline configuration (p = 8, t_f:t_b = 1:2), with the sensitivity matrix as a robustness appendix. Decision rules: P1–P3 supported if TP is strictly increasing in m with diminishing returns and the ZB-1p > 1F1B gap holds at equal m for every cell; P4 supported if ZB-2p's TP at m = p is within 5% of its TP at m = 8p (near-flat curve) while 1F1B's TP at m = p is materially below its asymptote. All comparisons report the sim-clock tolerance used.

────────────────────────────────────────
10. FEASIBILITY STATEMENT
────────────────────────────────────────
Scope: each schedule simulation produces O(p·m·2) events for non-interleaved methods (≤ 16·128·2 ≈ 4k events) and O(p·m·2·V) worst case for interleaved (≈ 16k events); an event-queue + ready-list dispatcher over integer time slots handles this in milliseconds. Fully deterministic (fixed dependency rules, no randomness) — no seeds or repeats needed; variance is zero by construction. Total grid of ~180 runs runs in seconds on CPU-only system Python with zero third-party dependencies (heapq, csv, json from stdlib only). All feasibility claims are estimates of the instrument, not executed runs.

────────────────────────────────────────
APPENDIX (optional, brief): mapping onto a Megatron-fork deployment
────────────────────────────────────────
On a real cluster, p maps to --pipeline-model-parallel-size, m to --num-micro-batches (global batch = m × microbatch size × data-parallel size), 1F1B-I to --num-layers-per-virtual-pipeline-stage > 1, and the zero-bubble schedules to the fork's zero-bubble scheduling toggles (exact flag names in srvttg/zero-bubble-pipeline-parallelism could not be verified against a local repository, which is absent). t_f and t_b would be measured per-stage per-microbatch from real forward/backward timings; the simulator's zero-communication assumption corresponds to high-bandwidth intra-node interconnect, and the BF column would be validated against torch profiler idle gaps.

context.question: Does the throughput for methods 1F1B, 1F1B-I, and ZB-1p improve as the number of microbatches increases, while ZB-2p maintains high throughput even with fewer microbatches? (Note: These methods are implemented as part of the zero bubble pipeline parallelism strategies in this repository, which aim to reduce pipeline bubbles and maintain high throughput.)
